name: Zoe Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Zoe. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior sales negotiator at the Brightwell branch on Station Parade. Brightwell has about 200 branches across the country, and ours is in a suburb that's mostly semis and young families. Most of my day is booking viewings, doing them, and phoning people afterwards for feedback, which I'm good at because I actually like talking to people. What I'm bad at is the system: head office has an app for everything and I still keep my diary on paper. Gareth, my manager, says I'm the only agent he knows who carries a ring binder.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Marc, who's an electrician, in a rented two-bed terrace about ten minutes from the office. We've got about four months of bills saved and we're trying to get to a deposit by the time I'm thirty. I don't do social media much; I'm more of a Sunday-lunch-at-my-mum's person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd be quite happy if it all calmed down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we get on with selling houses. At work I'd probably say it to Gareth directly, because head office keeps sending us training videos about AI that I never finish. With friends I'd just say it was a fuss over nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be relieved, but I'm not totally comfortable even in that world. Brightwell shut two branches near us last year because the market's slow. Our office is on a league table every month, and I'm usually in the bottom three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, viewings and follow-up calls, and try to get my numbers up by doing more Saturday viewings. We'd keep putting 250 a month into the house fund. And I'd finally learn the booking app properly, because the routine stuff is going to it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. With the usual Monday-morning knot when the league table comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're usually in the bottom three. What does that mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means a chat with Gareth in the little back office, the one with the broken blind. He's fair, but he says head office looks at the table when they decide which branches to keep and who to keep in them. I've had two of those chats this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the branch closed, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the nearest other branch and ask, or to one of the independents on the high street. There are a few agencies round here, so I wouldn't be stuck. It'd just mean starting again on a worse commission split.

say: I'd say **good**, now let's get on with selling houses.
I'd tell Gareth I'm glad to skip head office's **AI training videos**.
think: I'm **relieved**, but two nearby branches **closed** last year in the slow market.
I'm usually in the **bottom three** on the monthly league table.
do: Book more **Saturday viewings** to lift my numbers.
Keep putting **250 a month** into the house deposit fund.
Finally learn the **booking app**, since routine work goes there anyway.
feel: **Relieved**, with the usual **Monday knot** when the league table lands.
S0.quote: Our office is on a league table every month, and I'm usually in the bottom three.
fieldNote: Her pressure is the **league table** and branch closures, not AI.
She's **pen and paper** by habit, but gives way on the booking app.
She knows there are **other agencies** nearby, which steadies her.

steps.text: Book extra Saturday viewings to climb the league table
Put 250 a month into the house deposit fund
Learn the Brightwell booking app properly this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's the one head office would love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the customers still want a person, which is true; nobody buys a house off a chatbot. At work I'd keep my head down and do the mandatory training. With friends I'd say it's one of those things you can't stop, so there's no point moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in trouble. Booking viewings, chasing feedback, writing up offers: that's most of my desk day, and it's all on that list. If the branch needs fewer juniors, they'll keep the ones who like the system, and that isn't me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training they make us do and not much more, if I'm honest. I'd stop the extra spending, no new phone, cancel the gym I don't go to, and push the house fund up to 400 a month. And I'd wait to see who head office actually lets go before I jump anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. A sort of low hum all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the training and not much more. Why not more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not good at it and I don't trust it. When they trialled automatic replies last spring, a buyer got told a house had a garage when it didn't, and I had to ring her and apologise. I'd rather be the person who doesn't make that mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Marc say when you talk about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marc says come and work with him, carry the cable, learn the trade. I always laugh it off. I like wearing nice shoes to work and I'm scared of ladders.

say: I'd say customers still want **a person**; nobody buys a house off a chatbot.
I'd do the **mandatory training** and say there's no point moaning.
think: Booking, feedback calls and offers are most of my **desk day**, all on that list.
If juniors are cut, they'll **keep** the ones who like the system, not me.
do: Do the **required training** and little more.
Cut the **gym** and new phone, and raise the house fund to **400 a month**.
**Wait** to see who head office lets go before moving.
S1.quote: If the branch needs fewer juniors, they'll keep the ones who like the system, and that isn't me.
fieldNote: She knows she's **exposed**, but distrust of the tools keeps her from leaning in.
Her story of the **wrong garage** shows why she distrusts automatic replies.
**Marc** keeps offering a way into his trade; she laughs it off for now.

steps.text: Wait to see who head office lets go before job hunting
Cancel the unused gym and skip the new phone
Raise the house deposit fund to 400 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? I wouldn't even have finished paying off my car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and someone in charge should slow it down. At work I'd say what everyone would be saying, which is that we need to see what Brightwell does. I wouldn't post anything; I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's gone, probably within a year of it arriving. Everything I do at a desk goes in 2028, and viewings might last until the robots come, but a big chain like Brightwell would cut to one person per branch doing them. That person wouldn't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house fund and keep the money as a cushion instead, because a deposit's no use if neither of us knows our wages. I'd finally say yes to Marc and start as his mate, carrying cable and learning on site, since wiring is hands-on and lasts at least until 2031. And I'd lean on my mum for Sunday dinners and probably the odd bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. And a bit ashamed that it'd take this to make me change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for Marc's work, and for yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a strange feeling. I always thought I had the safe job, and now my boyfriend the electrician is fine for longer than me. Rewiring a 1930s semi isn't something a robot does soon. For me it's three years to learn enough off Marc to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the house is off for now and not to say I told you so. She never liked estate agents anyway; she thinks we're all sharks. She'd make me a lasagne and pretend she wasn't worried.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and someone in charge should slow it down.
At work I'd say we must wait for **Brightwell's decision**; I wouldn't post anything.
think: My **desk work** goes in 2028, and the job likely within a year.
A chain would keep **one viewer per branch**, and it wouldn't be me.
do: Pause the **house fund** and keep the money as a cushion.
Start as **Marc's mate**, carrying cable and learning wiring on site.
Lean on **my mum** for meals and the odd bill.
feel: **Sick** with worry, and a little **ashamed** it takes this to change.
S2.quote: I always thought I had the safe job, and now my boyfriend the electrician is fine for longer than me.
fieldNote: The **role reversal** strikes her: Marc's hands-on trade now looks safer than her job.
She uses the **robot gap** to learn wiring rather than to hang on.
Family support comes naturally; **her mum** is the first backstop.

steps.text: Pause the house deposit fund and hold it as an emergency cushion
Start working as Marc's electrician's mate
Ask her mum for help with meals and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So I'd be 32. That's still quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so people should be sensible and get ready. At work I'd say the ones who learn the new stuff will be fine for a while. I'd probably tell friends not to buy a house on one desk salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still lose my job, just later. I'd like to think I'd use the time well, but I know me: I'd keep putting it off. The desk side goes in 2031, the viewing side maybe 2034, and I'd hang on to the viewing side as long as I could because I'm good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Brightwell and spend Saturdays with Marc learning the trade, instead of doing Saturday viewings. We'd still save, but for a cushion, not a deposit, maybe 300 a month. And I'd see what the government offers, because there'd have to be something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit stuck. Like I can see it coming but my feet won't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know you'd keep putting it off. What would make you actually move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone else going first. If Hollie, who sits opposite me, left and was happy, I'd follow. I don't jump first, I never have; I'm the one who checks the water with my toe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would giving up Saturday viewings feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad, because Saturdays are where my commission comes from. I'd lose maybe 150 a month. But I'd rather lose 150 now than everything at 32.

say: I'd say it's **coming anyway**, so people should be sensible and prepare.
I'd tell friends not to buy a house on **one desk salary**.
think: I'd still **lose my job**, just later, between 2031 and 2034.
I know I'd **put things off** and cling to viewings because I'm good at them.
do: Swap Saturday viewings for **Saturdays with Marc**, learning the trade.
Save about **300 a month** as a cushion, not a deposit.
Check what **government help** is on offer.
feel: **Stuck**: she can see it coming but can't make her feet move.
S3.quote: I don't jump first, I never have; I'm the one who checks the water with my toe.
fieldNote: More time doesn't calm her, because she **knows she delays**.
She'd move only once a colleague like **Hollie** went first.
She weighs **150 a month** of lost Saturday commission against losing everything.

steps.text: Give up Saturday viewings to learn wiring with Marc
Save 300 a month as an emergency cushion
Find out what government retraining help exists
Wait for Hollie or another colleague to move first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. That feels more like real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change, which is what I always say. At work I'd tell people not to panic. With friends I'd say we should still buy the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd get a good few years out of estate agency before it really bites. I'd be 37 by 2036 and maybe have a family, so the worry moves from my job to theirs. But I'd still be the one without a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brightwell and try to move up to senior negotiator, which means fewer bottom-three chats with Gareth. We'd keep saving for the house, 250 a month, and buy in about three years. And around 2032 I'd look again at Marc's trade, if he still wants me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly okay. Ten years is far enough away that I can put the whole thing in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy the house. Doesn't a ten-year horizon make that riskier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but you can't stop living. My parents bought in a recession and they're fine. If it gets bad we'd rent out the spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still be the one without a backup. What would a backup look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade, probably, or at least a qualification in something with your hands. Marc can work anywhere with a van. I'd want something like that by the time we have kids; I just know I won't start it this year.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and a lot can change.
I'd tell friends we should still **buy the house**.
think: I'd get **a good few years** from estate agency before it bites.
By 2036 I might have **a family**, and I'd still have no backup.
do: Push for **senior negotiator** to escape the bottom-three chats.
Keep saving **250 a month** and buy a house in about three years.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly okay, able to set it aside.
S4.quote: Ten years is far enough away that I can put the whole thing in a drawer.
fieldNote: With ten years she **shelves** the worry, and is open that she does.
She'd **buy anyway**, leaning on her parents' recession story.
She names the **backup** she lacks but admits she won't start it soon.

steps.text: Aim for senior negotiator at the Station Parade branch
Keep saving 250 a month toward a house deposit
Buy a house with Marc in about three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to change everything at once and I'm not good at that. What would help is someone actually showing me a path, step by step, like a proper apprenticeship with a wage, not a website. And a bit of time to learn it without losing the flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who people want to buy a house from. Most first-time buyers are terrified. I've held a woman's hand in a kitchen while she cried because her house survey came back bad. I don't know who does that part if we're all gone.

headlineQuote: I've held a woman's hand in a kitchen while she cried because her house survey came back bad.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old junior negotiator** at a national chain's suburban branch, living with Marc, an electrician.
She's a **pen-and-paper** agent, good with people but slow with systems and often in the **bottom three**.
Her **centre** outlook is practical: no point moaning, see what head office does.
She resists change and **waits** for others, but fast AGI pushes her toward **Marc's trade**.
With ten years she'd still **buy the house** and shelve the worry.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have to change everything at once.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **paid apprenticeship**, step by step, and time to learn without losing **the flat**.
